scenarios.label: — Show all four equally —
scenarios.why: Click any cell with a dotted underline to see the source behind that specification.

scenarios.label: First circuits, youngest builders
scenarios.why: Untethered, nothing to plug into the wall, and a flattened pack costs about a dollar. Do supervise it: a shorted alkaline pack still gets hot enough to matter.

scenarios.label: Most classroom work
scenarios.why: Steady 5 V, a switch, an indicator light, and a documented current limit — and at about two dollars it is the part you would rather lose than the wall adapter.

scenarios.label: One long project at a desk
scenarios.why: The regulation happens inside a sealed, safety-tested brick. Its weakness is that it is the expensive thing on the bench when something shorts.

scenarios.label: Fault-finding, older students
scenarios.why: Dial the current limit down to 100 mA and a shorted board simply sits there at 0 V instead of cooking. The knob is the safety feature.

rows.name: 3 × AA Battery Pack
rows.safetyNote: Self-contained and low voltage, but a fresh alkaline pack is not the harmless thing it is often assumed to be.
rows.bestFor: First circuits, and anything that has to be carried around.

voltage.detail: Three alkaline cells in series at the datasheet nominal voltage of 1.5 V each. In practice a fresh pack reads nearer 4.7 V and sags steadily as the cells discharge — batteries have no regulator holding the voltage steady.

short.detail: The datasheet gives a fresh cell 150–300 mΩ of internal resistance. Three in series is 0.45–0.9 Ω, so 4.5 V across a dead short starts at roughly 5–10 A before the cells sag and heat up. Nothing switches off — the current falls only because the battery is exhausting itself.
short.alsoQuote: current flowing can be high enough to melt the plastic holders and insulation of the wires too

limit.detail: There is no regulator and no protection device in a battery holder. The only thing limiting the current is the chemistry of the cells themselves.

cost.detail: Holders run near a dollar each in ten-packs, and the cells are a bulk-store purchase. A short costs you the cells, not the holder.

rows.name: USB Wall Charger
rows.safetyNote: The mains-voltage part is sealed inside a safety-tested brick. What varies is the quality of what comes out.
rows.bestFor: A project that lives on one desk, near an outlet.

voltage.detail: USB fixes the bus voltage at 5 V. A port supplying a full-power device must stay between 4.75 V and 5.25 V — that is 5 V ± 5%. A charger is not adjustable: 5 V is what you get.
voltage.quote: a minimum VBUS of 4.75 V is specified with a maximum of 5.25V

short.detail: A reputable charger current-limits or shuts down and recovers when you clear the fault. A cheap unbranded one may do that, may sag, or may fail outright. There is no single number to quote here, because the population of chargers is not uniform — so this book does not print one.

limit.detail: Whatever the manufacturer built in. You cannot set it, see it, or change it from outside the case.

cost.detail: Bought ten at a time. Cheap in bulk — but replacing one means the charger died, and that is a part you would rather not be feeding into a shorted breadboard in the first place.

rows.name: MB102 Power Module
rows.safetyNote: Documented current limiting and thermal shutdown inside the regulator — and no fuse on the board. Protected is not the same as fused.
rows.bestFor: Most classroom work. Cheap enough to be the part that dies.

voltage.detail: The board carries two AMS1117 fixed regulators, the -5.0 and the -3.3, and a jumper picks which one feeds each power rail. Feed the barrel jack 7.5–9 V: the regulator needs about 1.3 V more at its input than it puts out, and every volt above that leaves as heat.

short.value: Limits at 0.9–1.5 A, then shuts down hot
short.detail: The regulator clamps the fault current and then switches itself off once the junction passes 165 °C, recovering when it cools. That is real protection — but it works by getting hot, and in the SOT-223 package the chip is rated for only 1.2 W. Shorting a 9 V-fed module asks it to burn roughly 10 W. It survives by cycling on and off.
short.quote: protected against short circuit and thermal overloads
short.alsoQuote: junction temperature exceed 165°C at the sense point

limit.detail: The datasheet specifies the current limit as 900 mA minimum, 1100 mA typical, 1500 mA maximum. You cannot adjust it — but unlike the charger, you can look it up.

cost.detail: This is the number that matters most. It is cheap enough to keep spares in the drawer, so a student short costs fifteen seconds and two dollars rather than a lost lesson.

rows.name: Bench Supply, Adjustable Limit
rows.safetyNote: The only supply here where you decide in advance how much current a fault is allowed to draw.
rows.bestFor: A teacher's bench, and fault-finding a board that misbehaves.

voltage.detail: You dial the voltage you want. In constant-voltage mode the supply holds that value and the load decides how much current it draws — until the current hits the limit you set.
voltage.quote: in CV mode, the output voltage equals the voltage setting value and the output current is determined by the load

short.detail: Short the output and the supply slides into constant-current mode: it holds the current at your setting and lets the voltage fall to whatever the fault demands — near zero for a dead short. Set 100 mA and a shorted board draws exactly 100 mA and stays cold.
short.quote: when the load current is greater than the current setting value, the power supply will switch to CC output mode automatically

limit.detail: This is the whole point of the instrument. The current knob is not a readout — it is the protection, chosen by you before you power up.
limit.quote: the output current equals the current setting value and the output voltage is determined by the load

cost.detail: A shared bench instrument, not a per-student item. One for the room is a reasonable purchase; twenty are not.

footnote: Board-level details of the MB102 itself — that it carries no fuse, and that its only board-level protection is a reverse-polarity diode — come from published teardowns rather than a manufacturer datasheet, because the MB102 is a generic module with no single manufacturer. Regulator specifications above are from the AMS1117 datasheet and are solid; board specifications vary between sellers. Verify your own board if the details matter.
